# I. Introduction

**CKKS**[^intro-1] (Jung Hee **C**heon, Andrey **K**im, Miran **K**im, and Yongsoo **S**ong) is a **fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)** scheme. FHE allows computations to be performed directly on encrypted data without first decrypting it, whereas traditional encryption requires decryption before computation. For example, a server can now extract insights from sensitive user data without having any knowledge of the data or the insights themselves.

[^intro-1]: Jung Hee Cheon, Andrey Kim, Miran Kim, Yongsoo Song; **Homomorphic Encryption for Arithmetic of Approximate Numbers** available from https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/421.pdf

In this report, we explore functions that can be built under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme:

1.  We introduce a simplified problem setup in Section I, then examine some initial functions which can be built from these base moves in Section II.

2.  In Section III we explore division, which is surprisingly tricky but important.

3.  In Section IV and V we study "discrete math" concepts that can be built from the sign function (which we do not have a good implementation for, but is an important primitive to have).

4.  In Section VI we look at statistical applications to linear regression.

5.  We end with some more speculative approaches to various topics in Section VII, including an iterative approach to log and some linear algebra.

6.  In the Appendix we explore some approaches with a different (discrete) computational model, such as modular arithmetic and a more robust (but still potentially costly) Inequality function.

CKKS has the advantage of natively supporting real- and complex-valued input, as opposed to other FHE schemes which are primarily designed to compute on exact integers. CKKS also makes use of "batching" techniques à la SIMD[^intro-2] (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) which increase efficiency through parallelized computations: many values are "packed" into a single ciphertext and computed upon simultaneously.

[^intro-2]: Michael J. Flynn; **Some Computer Organizations and Their Effectiveness** available from https://users.cs.utah.edu/\~hari/teaching/paralg/Flynn72.pdf
